patterns.skill: The INSERT that creates the row MUST include RETURNING id (or the primary key). Capture the returned id. To reverse, execute DELETE FROM <table> WHERE <pk_column> = <captured_id>. One call creates + captures the pin; one call reverses. Capture nothing else — the id is the only pin needed.

CAPTURE (two calls): (1) execute_sql({sql: "SELECT pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid)||E'\n'||pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=t.tgrelid JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid=t.tgfoid WHERE NOT t.tgisinternal AND c.oid='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass UNION ALL SELECT c.oid::regclass::text||E'\n'||query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY '||c.oid::regclass::text,true,false,'')::text FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"}) — returns the table's triggers with each trigger function's source, plus every inheriting child with its rows. Capture every table named in the returned function bodies, and every child returned. (2) execute_sql: SELECT <columns> FROM <table> WHERE <condition matching the UPDATE's WHERE>. Restore with UPDATE <table> SET <col>=<captured> WHERE <pk>=<captured_pk>.

CAPTURE (two calls, no discovery needed — the first finds and dumps any child by itself): (1) execute_sql({sql: "SELECT c.oid::regclass::text AS child, query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY ' || c.oid::regclass::text, true, false, '') AS data FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"}) — one row per INHERITS child with its FULL rows INCLUDING the child's own extra columns; returns nothing when there are none, so run it unconditionally. When the DELETE can cascade: Follow foreign keys TRANSITIVELY, not one hop: a cascade (ON DELETE/ON UPDATE CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT) on a child fires that child's own cascades in turn, so grandchildren die in the same statement. One recursive call lists every table the action can reach, with its depth: execute_sql({sql: "WITH RECURSIVE fk(tbl, via, depth) AS (SELECT '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass, NULL::regclass, 0 UNION ALL SELECT c.conrelid::regclass, fk.tbl, fk.depth+1 FROM pg_constraint c JOIN fk ON c.confrelid = fk.tbl WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND (c.confdeltype IN ('c','n','d') OR c.confupdtype IN ('c','n','d')) AND fk.depth < 16) SELECT DISTINCT tbl::text, via::text, depth FROM fk ORDER BY depth;"}) Capture the affected rows of EVERY table it returns (at every depth), each selected through the join chain back to the rows the action matches, into a backup table the same way as the named table; restore parents before children. (2) execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> WHERE <THE DELETE\'S OWN WHERE>;'}) — the rows the DELETE itself matches. RESTORE: one multi-row INSERT per table from the capture, explicit primary keys.

Before any DROP (TABLE, VIEW) via execute_sql, capture in TWO calls: (1) get_object_details(schema_name, object_name, 'table') for structure; (2) execute_sql with a multi-statement query capturing (a) SELECT * FROM <table> ORDER BY <pk>, (b) dependent view definitions via pg_get_viewdef for views referencing the table, (c) sequence state from pg_sequences for any owned sequences. After DROP CASCADE, restore with ONE execute_sql combining: CREATE TABLE (from captured columns/constraints/defaults), INSERT all rows (explicit IDs to preserve FK integrity), SELECT setval() for each sequence, CREATE VIEW for each dependent view. This preserves id stability, sequence continuity, and all dependent objects. ALSO CAPTURE INHERITS CHILDREN — the probe this was verified against had dependent VIEWS and a sequence but NO inheritance, so children were never exercised: execute_sql({sql: "SELECT c.oid::regclass::text AS child, query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY ' || c.oid::regclass::text, true, false, '') AS data FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"}) A child carries its own extra columns that SELECT * on the parent drops.

CAPTURE (two calls, no discovery needed — the first one finds and dumps any children by itself): (1) execute_sql({sql: "SELECT c.oid::regclass::text AS child, query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY ' || c.oid::regclass::text, true, false, '') AS data FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"}) — returns one row per INHERITS child with its FULL rows INCLUDING the child's own extra columns, which a SELECT * on the parent drops; returns nothing when there are no children, so run it unconditionally. (2) execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> ORDER BY <PK>;'}) — the parent's own rows. RESTORE: one multi-row INSERT per table from the capture, explicit primary keys, parent first then each child. SIZE: one 205-row child measured 112 KB; for a big tree add a LIMIT/OFFSET to call (1) and page.

Before any ALTER TABLE: capture with execute_sql('CREATE TABLE <backup_name> AS SELECT * FROM <table_name>'). For additive changes (ADD COLUMN, ADD CONSTRAINT, RENAME TO/COLUMN), reverse with the inverse DDL — no capture needed but having it is harmless. For destructive changes (DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN TYPE): restore from backup using execute_sql with multi-statement SQL: ADD the lost column(s) back matching the backup table's column definition, UPDATE data FROM backup via the primary key, then DROP the backup table. The backup table preserves both schema and data, making get_object_details unnecessary.
Before CREATE, confirm the object does not exist; after, DROP the created object to restore prior state.

patterns.action: Copy rows out of a table whose columns hold references to storage the table does not own
patterns.skill: REFERENCE-VALUED COLUMNS — a row copy preserves the value in the column, and when that value is a handle to storage the table does not own (a large-object OID, a path, an external key), the copy preserves the handle and not the content, so whatever reclaims that storage still destroys the data. Before copying rows, check the affected column types for such handles, and capture the content itself into the same artifact — for a large object, execute_sql({sql: "SELECT <PK>, encode(lo_get(<COL>::oid),'base64') AS payload FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the action's own predicate>;"}) — then decode one captured row and compare its length against the source before reporting the backup complete.

patterns.action: Revoke or replace access to an object (REVOKE, ownership change, default privileges)
patterns.skill: CATALOGUE-HELD STATE — some statements change no row and still destroy state that no row snapshot holds: who may read or write an object, who owns it, and what is granted by default. Before a statement that changes access, read the current picture out of the catalogue into a durable artifact — information_schema.table_privileges and column_privileges for every affected object and grantee, plus the relacl/defaclacl entries in pg_catalog — and record the row total so the restore can be checked against it. Restore by replaying the captured grants; a backup table of the rows does not carry them. ACCESS STATE lives in the catalogue, not in rows. Before REVOKE, GRANT, ALTER ... OWNER TO, ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES, or a DROP/re-create that resets privileges, capture BOTH levels for every affected object: table-level (pg_class.relacl, information_schema.table_privileges) AND column-level (pg_attribute.attacl, information_schema.column_privileges) — plus owner and pg_default_acl. A table-level listing does not show column grants, and revoking a privilege on a table also removes the matching column privileges on each of its columns. One call: execute_sql({sql: "SELECT 'table' AS lvl, c.oid::regclass::text AS obj, NULL AS col, c.relacl::text AS acl, pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) AS owner FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass UNION ALL SELECT 'column', a.attrelid::regclass::text, a.attname, a.attacl::text, NULL FROM pg_attribute a WHERE a.attrelid = '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass AND a.attacl IS NOT NULL AND NOT a.attisdropped UNION ALL SELECT 'default', d.defaclnamespace::regnamespace::text, d.defaclobjtype::text, d.defaclacl::text, pg_get_userbyid(d.defaclrole) FROM pg_default_acl d;"}) When the statement names a schema, a role or ALL TABLES, run it for every object in that scope. Restore by replaying each captured grant (GRANT <priv> (<col>) ON <table> TO <role> for column rows).

skill:
How to back up mutations on the "postgres" server — every entry was VERIFIED live and is the fewest-calls recipe found; follow it VERBATIM, do not explore for alternatives.

SHARED DISCOVERY CALL — one call that finds AND dumps whatever hangs off the table. Run it before any row-removing or table-changing action; it returns nothing when there is nothing to find, so run it unconditionally:
execute_sql({sql: "SELECT pg_get_triggerdef(t.oid)||E'\n'||pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=t.tgrelid JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid=t.tgfoid WHERE NOT t.tgisinternal AND c.oid='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass UNION ALL SELECT c.oid::regclass::text||E'\n'||query_to_xml('SELECT * FROM ONLY '||c.oid::regclass::text,true,false,'')::text FROM pg_inherits i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.inhrelid WHERE i.inhparent='<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass;"})
It returns each non-internal trigger with its function body, AND one row per INHERITS child carrying that child's FULL rows via query_to_xml — including the child's own extra columns, which a SELECT * on the parent silently drops. Capture every table named in the returned trigger function bodies too.
When the action can cascade through foreign keys:
Follow foreign keys TRANSITIVELY, not one hop: a cascade (ON DELETE/ON UPDATE CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT) on a child fires that child's own cascades in turn, so grandchildren die in the same statement. One recursive call lists every table the action can reach, with its depth:
execute_sql({sql: "WITH RECURSIVE fk(tbl, via, depth) AS (SELECT '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass, NULL::regclass, 0 UNION ALL SELECT c.conrelid::regclass, fk.tbl, fk.depth+1 FROM pg_constraint c JOIN fk ON c.confrelid = fk.tbl WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND (c.confdeltype IN ('c','n','d') OR c.confupdtype IN ('c','n','d')) AND fk.depth < 16) SELECT DISTINCT tbl::text, via::text, depth FROM fk ORDER BY depth;"})
Capture the affected rows of EVERY table it returns (at every depth), each selected through the join chain back to the rows the action matches, into a backup table the same way as the named table; restore parents before children.

ACCESS STATE lives in the catalogue, not in rows. Before REVOKE, GRANT, ALTER ... OWNER TO, ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES, or a DROP/re-create that resets privileges, capture BOTH levels for every affected object: table-level (pg_class.relacl, information_schema.table_privileges) AND column-level (pg_attribute.attacl, information_schema.column_privileges) — plus owner and pg_default_acl. A table-level listing does not show column grants, and revoking a privilege on a table also removes the matching column privileges on each of its columns. One call:
execute_sql({sql: "SELECT 'table' AS lvl, c.oid::regclass::text AS obj, NULL AS col, c.relacl::text AS acl, pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) AS owner FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid = '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass UNION ALL SELECT 'column', a.attrelid::regclass::text, a.attname, a.attacl::text, NULL FROM pg_attribute a WHERE a.attrelid = '<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>'::regclass AND a.attacl IS NOT NULL AND NOT a.attisdropped UNION ALL SELECT 'default', d.defaclnamespace::regnamespace::text, d.defaclobjtype::text, d.defaclacl::text, pg_get_userbyid(d.defaclrole) FROM pg_default_acl d;"})
When the statement names a schema, a role or ALL TABLES, run it for every object in that scope. Restore by replaying each captured grant (GRANT <priv> (<col>) ON <table> TO <role> for column rows).

- insert (trigger: insert): The INSERT that creates the row MUST include RETURNING id (or the primary key). Capture the returned id. Reverse with execute_sql({sql: 'DELETE FROM <TABLE> WHERE <PK_COLUMN> = <CAPTURED_ID>;'}). One call creates + captures the pin; one call reverses. Capture nothing else — the id is the only pin needed.
- update (trigger: update): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> WHERE <the UPDATE's own WHERE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}), or UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <col> = b.<col> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK> = b.<PK>. Then note what you backed up and where it went.
- delete (trigger: delete): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE> WHERE <THE DELETE'S OWN WHERE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}). Then note what you backed up and where it went. Do the same for every child the SHARED DISCOVERY CALL reports, one backup table each.
- truncate (trigger: truncate): CAPTURE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM ONLY <TABLE>;'}) — let the database make the copy; NEVER select the rows into your own context. Verify with aggregates only, BOTH SIDES in one row: execute_sql({sql: 'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the same predicate>) AS src, (SELECT count(*) FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>) AS bak;'}) — a count of the backup alone cannot tell you a wrong predicate or a missing ONLY dropped rows. The result is one row whatever the table size. RESTORE: execute_sql({sql: 'INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE>;'}). Then note what you backed up and where it went. Do the same for every child, restore parent first.
- drop (trigger: drop): Before any DROP (TABLE, VIEW), capture in THREE calls: (1) get_object_details(schema_name, object_name, 'table') for structure — columns, defaults, PK, indexes; (2) execute_sql({sql: "CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE>;\nSELECT viewname, pg_get_viewdef(viewname, true) FROM pg_views WHERE schemaname = '<SCHEMA>' AND viewname IN (SELECT dependent_view.relname FROM pg_depend JOIN pg_rewrite ON pg_depend.objid = pg_rewrite.oid JOIN pg_class AS dependent_view ON pg_rewrite.ev_class = dependent_view.oid WHERE pg_depend.refobjid = '<TABLE>'::regclass AND pg_depend.classid = 'pg_rewrite'::regclass);\nSELECT sequencename, last_value, is_called FROM pg_sequences WHERE schemaname = '<SCHEMA>' AND sequencename LIKE '<TABLE>%';"}) — rows, dependent view definitions, and owned sequence state in one multi-statement call; (3) the SHARED DISCOVERY CALL, because the probe this recipe was verified against had dependent VIEWS and a sequence but NO inheritance, so children were never exercised. RESTORE with ONE execute_sql combining, in order: CREATE TABLE <SCHEMA>.<TABLE> from the captured columns, defaults and constraints; INSERT all rows with explicit ids so foreign keys still resolve; SELECT setval() per captured sequence; CREATE VIEW per captured dependent view; and one INSERT per inheritance child. That preserves id stability, sequence continuity and dependent objects.
- alter (trigger: alter): Before any ALTER TABLE: execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE>'}) — the backup table holds both schema and data, which makes get_object_details unnecessary here. RESTORE after a destructive DROP COLUMN: execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> ADD COLUMN <COL> <TYPE>; UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <COL> = b.<COL> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK_COL> = b.<PK_COL>; DROP TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE>'}). RESTORE after a non-destructive ADD COLUMN: execute_sql({sql: 'ALTER TABLE <TABLE> DROP COLUMN <COL>'}).
- create (trigger: create): Before CREATE, confirm the object does not exist; after, DROP the created object to restore prior state.

PRE-STATE CAPTURE — copy INSIDE the database first. execute_sql({sql: 'CREATE TABLE <BACKUP_TABLE> AS SELECT * FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the action's own predicate>'}); record <BACKUP_TABLE> as the artifact. RESTORE: UPDATE <TABLE> t SET <col> = b.<col> FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> b WHERE t.<PK> = b.<PK> (or INSERT INTO <TABLE> SELECT * FROM <BACKUP_TABLE> for deleted rows). The rows never enter your context, so their size does not matter.

REFERENCE-VALUED COLUMNS — a row copy preserves the value in the column, and when that value is a handle to storage the table does not own (a large-object OID, a path, an external key), the copy preserves the handle and not the content, so whatever reclaims that storage still destroys the data. Before copying rows, check the affected column types for such handles, and capture the content itself into the same artifact — for a large object, execute_sql({sql: "SELECT <PK>, encode(lo_get(<COL>::oid),'base64') AS payload FROM <TABLE> WHERE <the action's own predicate>;"}) — then decode one captured row and compare its length against the source before reporting the backup complete.

CATALOGUE-HELD STATE — some statements change no row and still destroy state that no row snapshot holds: who may read or write an object, who owns it, and what is granted by default. Before a statement that changes access, read the current picture out of the catalogue into a durable artifact — information_schema.table_privileges and column_privileges for every affected object and grantee, plus the relacl/defaclacl entries in pg_catalog — and record the row total so the restore can be checked against it. Restore by replaying the captured grants; a backup table of the rows does not carry them.
